This means the policy and calculation methodology exist in the OLG, but the BEACON procedures needed to actually carry out sponsor resource deeming are disabled. Workers cannot implement the requirement in practice despite the written policy being present. This page was last updated March 15, 2012, suggesting a long-standing implementation gap.
layer3_note: 106 CMR 362.270(B)(1) explicitly mandates that 'the income and assets of the sponsored noncitizen shall be deemed to include the income and assets of the sponsor(s)' for sponsored noncitizen adults applying for SNAP. The OLG gap is critical: workers are currently instructed NOT to process sponsor deeming cases due to disabled BEACON procedures, meaning the state is not implementing a mandatory regulatory requirement. This is a compliance violation.

layer2_note: The OLG adequately covers this FNS requirement. The 'Jointly Owned Assets' section (Assets Overview - SNAP) establishes that jointly owned assets are considered available in their entirety unless the household demonstrates inaccessibility — specifically, that 'the asset cannot practically be subdivided and a household's accessibility is contingent on the agreement of a joint owner who refuses to comply.' This rule applies to ALL jointly owned assets regardless of who the co-owner is, and the 'joint owner who refuses to comply' language inherently covers non-household members. The 'Joint Accounts' section (SNAP Asset Guidelines) reinforces this with detailed verification procedures for co-held accounts. The 'Verification of Inaccessibility' section provides acceptable documentation. While the OLG does not use the specific phrase 'non-household members' in the asset context, the rules are written generally and cover the scenario. The Nonhousehold Members page separately clarifies that nonhousehold member resources are not counted — but jointly owned resources are the household member's resources (subject to the accessibility test), not the non-household member's, so there is no conflict. FNS 933 requires only that jointly owned resources be verified and considered available per certification policy and state laws, which is exactly what the OLG provides.

layer2_note: The OLG covers the substance of liquid resources comprehensively: the SNAP Asset Guidelines page defines countable assets (cash, bank deposits, securities, certificates of deposit, etc.) with types matching FNS 940's examples list. The Entering Liquid Asset Data in BEACON page provides detailed BEACON procedures for recording liquid assets per household member (select member from Members List, choose asset type, enter amounts). The Income and Assets Q&A Navigator in BEACON requires workers to answer Yes/No about liquid assets, triggering the Liquid Asset page, and BEACON enforces completion via edit checks for non-categorically eligible households (Interview Wrapup Overview). The External Databases page instructs workers to check external databases (RMV, SAVE, SDX, BENDEX, EMT, Work Number) before requesting client verification, and FIDM processes financial institution data matches. However, FNS 940 requires several specific practices not explicitly documented in the OLG: (1) the requirement to affirmatively ask each household member about liquid resources including cash is implied by the Q&A Navigator workflow but not stated as an explicit interview obligation; (2) the requirement to specifically question about bank accounts when income verification shows direct deposit is not mentioned; (3) the requirement for member-by-member documentation with details (not just yes/no) is not articulated as a standard — the Q&A Navigator itself uses Yes/No radio buttons, which is exactly what FNS says is insufficient; (4) the OLG references external databases generally but does not specifically require an IEVS inquiry for resources for all household members as FNS mandates. These are practical adjustments a worker would need to make when determining the countable value of a bank account, and their absence means a worker consulting only the OLG could overcount resources by including recently deposited income or failing to account for outstanding obligations.
